128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Won: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was Fred Rogers's gentle PBS children's show, running from 1968 to 2001, that mixed puppets, Make-Believe, and unhurried talk about feelings. This book argues the show was quietly doing philosophy: Rogers took children's wonder seriously, asked Socratic questions about who we are, and insisted every person is lovable just as they are. Essays trace his kinship with Plato, Aristotle, and Daoist thought, and probe what his puppets, silences, and 'posthuman' neighbors say about personhood, play, and community.
129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy: RuPaul's Drag Race is the Emmy-winning reality competition, running since 2009, in which drag queens battle through challenges and lip syncs until RuPaul crowns the next drag superstar. It is also a rich philosophical playground: what makes a good queen, and is fierceness a virtue? Essays bring Aristotle to the judging panel, speech-act theory to reading versus shade, Baudrillard to 'realness', and game theory to the All Stars elimination twist, while asking how gender, self-love, and authenticity get performed in the werkroom.
130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Ge: The Good Place was the NBC comedy (2016-2020) in which self-absorbed Eleanor Shellstrop wakes in a heaven she was never meant for, tutored by the indecisive ethics professor Chidi Anagonye. Unusually for a sitcom, philosophy is the show's actual vocabulary rather than a gag. Essays weigh its afterlife point system against Kant, Arendt, and Nietzsche, ask whether anyone can ever do enough good to deserve paradise, puzzle over the trolley problem and Chidi's indecision, and take seriously the question of whether hell is other people.
131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philoso: The Infinity Saga is Marvel Studios' interconnected run of superhero films that climaxed in Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame (2018-2019), when the titan Thanos wiped out half of all life with a snap of his fingers. A villain with a coherent argument invites hard questions. Was Thanos a consistent utilitarian? Do the Avengers' time-travel fixes gamble with other people's rights? Essays on grief, sacrifice, population ethics, and Tony Stark's final choice treat the blockbusters as serious tests of moral theory.
133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The C: Perry Mason, the courtroom drama starring Raymond Burr that ran from 1957 to 1966, adapted Erle Stanley Gardner's novels about a defense attorney whose clients are always innocent and whose cases always crack open in court. That tidy formula hides hard questions: was Mason actually good, or just lucky? Essays use moral luck and Kant to interrogate his record, compare him with Better Call Saul's Saul Goodman, weigh perjury against reasonable doubt, and draw on psychology to show why eyewitness testimony so often fails.
134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than H: KISS is the American rock band, famous since the mid-1970s for face paint, pyrotechnics, anthems, and the personas of the Demon, Starchild, Space Ace, and Catman. Beneath the spectacle the contributors find a workable philosophy: a steady message of self-belief and perseverance, Paul Stanley's hard-won examined life, and career bets made on Jamesian pragmatic faith rather than evidence. Essays also press the Ship of Theseus problem on a band that kept touring after its original members left, debunk the 'Knights in Satan's Service' rumor, and revisit KISS's disco detour.
136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want t: 30 Rock was Tina Fey's Emmy-winning NBC sitcom (2006-2013) about Liz Lemon, the harried head writer of a live sketch show, her corporate overlord Jack Donaghy, and the uncontrollable star Tracy Jordan. The book treats the writers' room as a philosophy seminar: Aristotle's three friendships illuminate Liz and Jack's odd alliance, Marx explains Liz's alienated workaholism, Confucius indicts the show's settled-for 'semi-virtue', and Appiah and Fanon frame Tracy's performance of race. Even Kenneth the page's rule-worship gets its own ethical audit.
137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is Lewis Carroll's 1865 classic - continued in Through the Looking-Glass and beloved through Disney's adaptation - about a girl who falls down a rabbit-hole into a world of grinning cats, mad tea parties, and backwards logic. Carroll was a logician, and the nonsense is rigorous. Essays read Alice's trial through Hobbes and Locke on consent and authority, the Mad Tea Party as Cold War deterrence strategy, the White Queen's jam rule as a problem of procrastination, and Wonderland's word games as lessons in how language can deceive.
138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Th: Alien began with Ridley Scott's 1979 masterpiece - a haunted-house horror film in space, with Sigourney Weaver's Ripley battling an almost perfect killing machine - and grew into a franchise of sequels, prequels, and androids. Its bleak corporate future is philosophically loaded. Are Ash, Bishop, and David persons or property? What does Weyland-Yutani owe the crews it marks expendable? Essays on moral status, Marx, care ethics, and cosmic horror find the Xenomorph saga says as much about us as about the monster.
139 - Arrested Development and Philosoph: Arrested Development is the acclaimed sitcom (2003-2006, later revived by Netflix) about the Bluths, a wealthy, wildly self-absorbed family whose patriarch's fraud leaves level-headed Michael to hold them together, alongside Gob's failed illusions, Tobias's obliviousness, and Buster's mother fixation. The family's serial self-deception is philosophical gold. Essays test Socrates' claim that the examined life is happiest - and find the Bluths thriving without it - read Gob through Sartre's bad faith and Buster through Freud, and ask what, exactly, makes George Michael's kiss with his cousin wrong.
